The deadline

February. The publisher wants the translation by 15 March. Ecaterina still has five chapters to translate, and her eyes fail her more and more often. Ana comes to see her and finds her at the kitchen table, with the magnifying glass and three dictionaries open.
Ecaterina, it’s eleven at night. Even if you only have a little left, you need to rest.
I can’t. Although I’ve already done fifteen chapters, I have five left, and the deadline is 15 March.
You could ask for another month. I’m sure the publisher will understand.
However much they understand, the book has to be in Madrid in May. Andrés can’t wait another month.
But your eyes…
My eyes don’t see much, although they still see enough. And however tired I am, when I translate I feel young.
In spite of everything, let me help you. I can read the text aloud to you while you write.
You? With that Madrid accent? Even so… I accept. And that’s although I’ve never let anyone touch my translations.
Then we start tomorrow. However much you protest, the light goes out at ten at night.
(smiling) You sound like my mother. All right. But I’ll translate the last chapter on my own.

a-UN-que: “au” as in “cow”, and “qu” = “k”.
“Aun” without an accent = even (“aun así”); “aún” with an accent = still, yet (“aún no”). They sound different: aun (one syllable), a-ÚN (two).
The first part (“Aunque…”) is said with a suspended tone, the second (“…voy a terminarlo”) falls firmly.
1. Aunque + indicative or subjunctive?
Aunque + INDICATIVE
Aunque + SUBJUNCTIVE
a real fact, new information
a hypothesis or a known fact considered unimportant
Aunque estoy cansada, sigo. (I am tired — I’m telling you.)
Aunque esté cansada, sigo. (Whether I am or not — it doesn’t matter.)
Aunque llueve, salimos. (It’s raining now.)
Aunque llueva mañana, saldremos. (It may rain.)
With the imperfect subjunctive the hypothesis is even less likely: «Aunque me pagaran el doble, no lo haría» (Even if they paid me double, I wouldn’t do it).
Learners tend to translate “although” always with the indicative. Think about what you mean: if it’s new information, indicative; if it’s an objection you’re dismissing, subjunctive.
2. Por mucho que, por más que, por muy… que
They express a strong concession (“however much…”). They almost always take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
However much you protest, the light goes out at ten.
However tired I am, when I translate I feel young.
However much of a hurry you’re in, check the text.
“Por muy” + adjective/adverb, but “por mucho/a/os/as” + noun (it agrees): «por muy difícil que sea», «por muchos problemas que haya».
3. A pesar de, si bien, aun así, y eso que
Construction / register
+ infinitive / noun

+ indicative (fact) / subjunctive (hypothesis)

si bien
+ indicative, formal
Si bien ve poco, todavía ve lo suficiente.
at the start of the clause
Ve poco. Aun así, traduce cada noche.
+ indicative, informal, at the end
No ha dormido, y eso que se acostó pronto.
aun + gerund
Aun estando cansada, terminó el capítulo.
“Y eso que” introduces a fact that should have led to a different result: it’s very expressive in speech.

Opinión: ¿Tienen futuro los traductores?
An opinion piece built on concessions. Notice how the author acknowledges the objections before countering them.
It’s true that machines translate better and better. Although ten years ago their mistakes made us laugh, today many technical texts are translated with almost no human intervention.
However, however advanced technology is, literature remains something else. A novel isn’t a list of data: it’s a voice, a rhythm, a silence between two sentences.
Although some publishers have already tried machine translation of novels, the results have been disappointing, even though the texts were revised afterwards.
However much machines advance, we will always need someone who understands why a sentence makes you cry. Even so, translators will have to learn to work with them.

Las últimas cinco páginas

For three weeks, Ecaterina’s kitchen became a translation workshop. Ana arrived every afternoon at six, after her classes, with bread, cheese and fruit, because she had discovered that Ecaterina forgot to eat when she was translating. They sat facing each other at the small table by the window. Ana read the Spanish text aloud, slowly, sentence by sentence. Ecaterina wrote the translation by hand in a notebook, holding the magnifying glass in her other hand.

Although Ecaterina had accepted the help, she didn’t make it easy for her. She corrected Ana’s pronunciation all the time. She told her she read too fast, that she swallowed her s’s like all Madrid people, that she didn’t respect the commas. Ana, however much it annoyed her, kept quiet and started again. She had understood that for Ecaterina, correcting was a form of affection.

They translated about four pages every evening. Some sentences took them hours. There was one, in chapter seventeen, that cost them a whole afternoon: “He gave her a book she wasn’t looking for and was left with a love he wasn’t expecting.” In Spanish it sounded like a song. In Romanian, however hard they tried, it sounded like washing-machine instructions. Ecaterina tried eleven versions. She didn’t like any of them.

Every evening before going to bed, Ecaterina called Madrid. Marta told her how her grandfather had spent the day. On some days, Andrés asked about the translation and wanted to know which chapter they had reached. On other days he didn’t ask anything. But even if he didn’t remember the translator’s name, he always remembered that someone in Bucharest was working on his story. “He says it’s as if someone were sewing him a made-to-measure coat,” Marta told her one evening.

It was Rosa Elena who found the solution, without knowing it. That afternoon she had come with Ana, because Mihai was on call at the hospital. While the two women argued, the little girl was drawing on the kitchen floor and singing in Romanian a song her grandmother Elena had taught her, a children’s song with simple rhymes. Ecaterina stopped writing and listened to her. Then she crossed out the eleven versions and wrote a twelfth, with the same rhythm as the song. That one she liked.

At the end of February, however, things started to get complicated. Ecaterina had a bad flu that kept her in bed for five days. Although the doctor had forbidden her to get up, Ana found her twice in the kitchen, in her nightdress, with a fever, trying to translate. The second time she got really angry. She took away the notebook, took away the magnifying glass and told her that, however much she loved Andrés, a dead translator would be no use to him at all.

Ecaterina looked at her in silence. Then she said she was right, even though she hated admitting anyone was right. She went back to bed without protesting. Ana stayed in the kitchen, looking at the notebook. Three chapters to go. Sixteen days left. She did the maths. Even if Ecaterina recovered quickly, it would be almost impossible to finish on time.

That night Ana sent a message to the club’s group chat. She explained the situation in a few lines. In less than an hour, everyone had replied. Domnul Dan, Andrei’s father, a bridge engineer and the most meticulous person Ana knew, offered to check the spelling and punctuation. Andrei offered to type up the notebooks, because Ecaterina wrote by hand and the publisher wanted the text in digital format. Costel wrote from Germany that he didn’t know how to translate, but he could bring soup.

And that was how, for the next two weeks, the whole club moved into Ecaterina’s flat. She translated from her bed, propped up on pillows, dictating quietly. Ana read the original. Andrei typed on the computer, sitting on the floor. Domnul Dan proofread at the kitchen table, with a red pencil and the seriousness of an examiner. And every Friday Costel turned up with a huge pot of meatball soup made by his neighbour, because he, however hard he tried, couldn’t cook.

For Domnul Dan, those two weeks had a special meaning. For years he hadn’t known how to talk to his son; between them there had been long silences, arguments about university, closed doors. Now they worked together every evening, one on the floor with the computer and the other at the table with the red pencil, passing pages to each other almost without a word. One evening Ana saw them laughing together at a typo. It was the first time she had seen them both laugh at the same time.

Mihai, for his part, took the opportunity to ask an ophthalmologist colleague to come and see Ecaterina. The doctor examined her right there in the kitchen, with a small torch, while she protested. He told her she had cataracts in both eyes and that, although the operation was simple, she shouldn’t have it before the trip to Madrid. Ecaterina answered that suited her perfectly, because she wanted to see Andrés’s face with her own eyes, even if it was blurred.

Costel’s soup became famous. It was made by his neighbour, Doamna Florica, a seventy-year-old widow who, when she found out who it was for, started adding something new every week: some herbs from the countryside, a piece of homemade bread, a handwritten note that said “For the translator, so she eats”. Ecaterina, who didn’t know her, sent her via Costel a book of Spanish recipes she had translated in 1984. Doamna Florica replied with another pot, even bigger.

There were difficult moments. One night Andrei’s computer froze and they almost lost two chapters. Another night Domnul Dan and Ecaterina argued for half an hour about a comma. Although both knew they were right, neither wanted to give in. In the end, Ana proposed a diplomatic solution: remove the comma and put a full stop. They both agreed, although neither of them was happy.

In spite of everything, the work was moving forward. On 10 March they finished chapter nineteen. Only the last one remained. Ecaterina, who had recovered from the flu by then, asked them to leave her alone. She reminded everyone of what she had said from the start: that she would translate the last chapter herself, without help. Nobody argued. That evening everyone went home at ten, for the first time in two weeks.

The last chapter of the novel was the shortest: only five pages. It told of the day the young foreign woman left Madrid without saying goodbye, and the bookseller found, the next morning, a book left behind on the counter. It was the chapter Ecaterina had avoided for months. Every time she reached it, she closed the book. Now she had no choice but to open it.

It took her three nights to translate five pages. Nobody knows exactly what happened on those nights. Ana called her every morning and Ecaterina always gave her the same answer: “I’m going slowly. Even though it’s only five pages.” Domnul Dan, who came by to collect the text on the 14th, said later that he had found her with swollen eyes, although she assured him it was from the magnifying glass.

On 15 March, at eleven fifty-eight at night, two minutes before the deadline, Andrei pressed the “send” button. The email with the complete translation went off to the publisher. Everyone was in Ecaterina’s kitchen: Ana, Andrei, Domnul Dan, Costel, who had arrived from Germany that very afternoon, and even Aunt Viorica, who had promised not to film anything and had kept her word, although with great effort.

Nobody clapped. They stayed staring at the screen in silence, as if they expected the email to come back. Then Costel took out of a bag a bottle of Romanian sparkling wine and seven plastic cups. They drank to the translation, to Andrés, to Marta, to the publisher, to Domnul Dan’s comma and, finally, to Rosa Elena’s children’s song, which had saved chapter seventeen.

The next morning, the editor in Bucharest replied. She wrote that she had started reading the translation at seven in the morning and hadn’t been able to stop. She said it was the best translation she had received in twenty years of work, even though she had published many famous translators. At the end, she asked whether Ecaterina wanted to add a dedication of her own in the Romanian edition, beneath the author’s.

Ecaterina thought about it for a whole day. She wrote several long sentences and crossed them all out, as she had done with the notebook before the video call. In the end she replied with just four words, which the editor put on the first page, in small print, under Marta’s: “For A., who waited.” When Ana read them, she had to step out onto the balcony for a moment, although it was very cold.

When everyone had gone, Ecaterina asked Ana to stay for a moment. She gave her the notebook with the last chapter, handwritten, full of crossings-out. She asked her to keep it. Ana asked why. Ecaterina replied that, however hard she tried, she couldn’t read it again, and she didn’t want to throw it away. “One day,” she added, “when I’m no longer here, give it to Rosa Elena. Tell her it was her song that taught me how to finish it.”

Ana put the notebook in her bag, next to Carmen’s frying pan that wasn’t there, next to Ion’s Leica that wasn’t there either, next to all the things her Romanian family had taught her to keep. She went down the stairs slowly. Outside, in the street, it was starting to rain. She thought that, although she was tired, although it was almost midnight, although she had a class at eight the next morning, she had never felt so awake.
